newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Agriculture Dept. launches anti-bias drive.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Agriculture Dept. launches anti-bias drive.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman announced a wide-ranging campaign on Friday to combat racial bias at the department, including a federal take-over of the 12,000 county employees who run its local offices.

Also on the to-do list is a speedy clean-up of long-standing complaints from minority farmers and department employees of discriminatory treatment, "a zero-tolerance policy for reprisals" and a policy to suspend foreclosure auctions in cases that allege loan discrimination.
"It is time to heal," Glickman said in a televised speech to employees. "We cannot change the past but we can and will set a new direction for the future of this department."

Black farmers picketed the department headquarters last fall to call attention to their complaints of unfair treatment. Glickman ordered a special review of the civil rights system as it affected farmers and employees.

The report, released on Friday, suggested 92 changes. Glickman said most were feasible and set a six-month deadline to implement them. He also appointed Pearlie Reed, the head of the review, as acting assistant secretary for administration.

Reed's report and a companion one by Inspector General Roger Viadero said there were 241 pending complaints from farmers and, at the start of this fiscal year, 1,391 complaints from employees. Many of the farmers' complaints were more than a year old.

Federalisation of the 12,000 county-level employees would be the most obvious change nationwide in the campaign if Congress consents. Currently, the Agriculture Department pays the salaries of the front-line workers but they are hired through a farmer-elected committee that oversees each office.
"The direct line of authority is not as clear as it ought to be," Glickman told reporters.

Legislation would be sent to Congress to federalise the work force and to empower the department to appoint two people to serve on the county committees as the voice of "underrepresented groups," Glickman said.
The committees now have three to five members. Congress rejected the idea of appointed members in 1994.
Spokesmen for the NAACP and the Department of Agriculture Coalition of Minority Employees said there was little in Glickman's plan to avenge past cases of discrmination.
"We don't talk about penalties," the NAACP's Leroy Warren Jr. said. "One punishment, one firing -- one example -- would make people change their minds."
The coalition's Lawrence Lucas said violators would not be held to the new zero-tolerance policy. "All I see right now is a piece of paper," Lucas said.
